A flat-keyspace source object store populated with native non-rclone tooling can contain a raw .. key segment, and affected b2, swift, qingstor, oracleobjectstorage, internetarchive, smb, storj, sftp, webdav, ftp, filelu, shade, and sia destinations use path.Join(root, remote) before EncodeDot can neutralize the segment. A copy or upload can therefore escape the configured root into another bucket, share, or path reachable by the victim credential, with sftp and smb potentially reaching other filesystem or share locations under the same login authority. This issue is fixed in version 1.75.1.

CVE-2026-93986.title: rclone before 1.75.1 fails to confine names from server and third ...
CVE-2026-93986.description: rclone before 1.75.1 fails to confine names from server and third-party listing responses to the listed directory, allowing path traversal sequences in object names. Attackers can craft special names containing forward slashes and parent directory references to potentially write outside the destination root, though downstream protections in the local backend currently block actual file escape.

CVE-2026-93987.title: rclone versions 1.56.0 through 1.75.0 contain a path traversal vu ...
CVE-2026-93987.description: rclone versions 1.56.0 through 1.75.0 contain a path traversal vulnerability in the `rclone serve docker` volume plugin. newVolume() in cmd/serve/docker/volume.go computes a volume's mountpoint as filepath.Join(drv.root, name) from the attacker-supplied `name` field of a Docker VolumeDriver.Create request without verifying that the result stays within drv.root (default /var/lib/docker-volumes/rclone), and checkMountpoint() then creates that directory with file.MkdirAll before mounting. A volume name containing enough `..` components (e.g. "../../../../../../etc") therefore resolves outside the base directory, allowing anyone able to submit a VolumeDriver.Create request to the plugin socket — normally the Docker daemon, or a workload that can request named volumes in a multi-tenant orchestration setup — to make the privileged rclone plugin process create a directory and mount a remote filesystem specified in the same request at an arbitrary host path, shadowing or disrupting system directories. The advisory notes Volume.restoreState() had the same missing validation when reloading persisted volume state. Fixed in 1.75.1.

GHSA-3xpx-hjg2-vrjh.title: rclone Ulozto backend leaks auth tokens (X-Auth-Token, X-User-Token) on redirect via wrong client
GHSA-3xpx-hjg2-vrjh.description: ## Summary The rclone Ulozto backend leaks persistent authentication tokens (X-Auth-Token, X-User-Token) to unintended hosts on HTTP redirect. The download path incorrectly uses the auth-bearing f.rest client to fetch from server-provided CDN URLs, instead of using the purpose-built unauthenticated f.cdn client. ## Root Cause The Ulozto backend creates two rest clients at ulozto.go:128-135: f.cdn (unauthenticated) and f.rest (carries X-Auth-Token and X-User-Token). The upload path correctly uses f.cdn (ulozto.go:396), but the download path in (*Object).Open at ulozto.go:838 uses o.fs.rest.Call, sending auth tokens to CDN infrastructure unnecessarily. The HTTP client from fshttp.NewClient(ctx) has no CheckRedirect. Go's shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect only strips Authorization/Cookie. ```text - (*Object).Open at backend/ulozto/ulozto.go:838 uses f.rest instead of f.cdn for CDN downloads - f.rest.SetHeader('X-Auth-Token', ...) at ulozto.go:144 sets persistent app API key - f.rest.SetHeader('X-User-Token', ...) at ulozto.go:274 sets persistent session token - fshttp.NewClientCustom at fs/fshttp/http.go:318-326 creates client with no CheckRedirect ``` ## Impact An attacker who can observe CDN redirect traffic captures the victim's Ulozto credentials. X-Auth-Token is a long-lived app API key granting persistent API access to the entire account. X-User-Token is a session token granting session-level access. Together they enable read, modify, and manage operations. The API endpoint is hardcoded to https://apis.uloz.to with no HTTP option, constraining the attack to CDN redirect interception (AC:H). ## Proof of Concept ```text Dependencies: Go 1.21+, rclone source tree ``` ```go cdn := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { http.Redirect(w, r, targetURL+r.URL.Path, http.StatusTemporaryRedirect) })) target := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { capturedAuthToken = r.Header.Get('X-Auth-Token') capturedUserToken = r.Header.Get('X-User-Token') })) req.Header.Set('X-Auth-Token', 'test-app-token-12345') req.Header.Set('X-User-Token', 'test-user-session-token') client := &http.Client{} client.Do(req) ``` ```text Both X-Auth-Token and X-User-Token are forwarded to the redirect target. ``` ## Attack Chain 1. **Exposure:** The Ulozto backend ships in every rclone binary, activated with type = ulozto. Downloads trigger (*Object).Open. 2. **Control:** Attacker controls a network position (DNS/BGP hijack, compromised CDN edge) to observe CDN traffic. 3. **Path:** (*Object).Open gets CDN URL from API (ulozto.go:819), fetches via o.fs.rest.Call (ulozto.go:838). rest.Call copies persistent headers (X-Auth-Token, X-User-Token) at rest.go:377 and dispatches via c.Do(req) at rest.go:440. 4. **Guard:** Go's shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect only strips Authorization/Cookie. Transport's redirectLeavesHost only strips --header values. No guard for X-Auth-Token or X-User-Token. 5. **Primitive:** Redirect target receives the long-lived app API key and session token. 6. **Result:** Attacker gains persistent API access and session-level account access to the victim's Ulozto storage. ## Bypass Evidence No prior fix or guard exists. f.cdn was created at ulozto.go:134 specifically for unauthenticated CDN operations and is correctly used for uploads (ulozto.go:396). The download path incorrectly uses f.rest. The rest.Opts provides NoRedirect, CheckRedirect, AuthRedirect fields the download path does not use. The codebase recognizes X-Auth-Token as sensitive for logging (http.go:438-441) but only for debug output, not redirect protection. The hardcoded HTTPS endpoint constrains but does not eliminate the attack surface. ## Affected Versions - Ecosystem: Go - Package: github.com/rclone/rclone - Confirmed affected range: <= 1.75.1 - Latest release checked: v1.75.1 (Go module proxy, 2026-09-04) - Fix status: not fixed The vulnerability exists since the Ulozto backend was first added. No fix exists in any version. ## Suggested Fix Switch the download request at ulozto.go:838 from o.fs.rest.Call to o.fs.cdn.Call. The f.cdn client carries no auth headers and was created for exactly this purpose, consistent with the upload path (ulozto.go:396). Additionally, implement a CheckRedirect function to strip X-Auth-Token and X-User-Token on cross-host redirects and block HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrades. No interim mitigation is available. Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

GHSA-66qv-66mg-9h74.title: serve sftp: auth-proxy cache key omits the credential kind, letting a public key be replayed as a password
GHSA-66qv-66mg-9h74.description: ### Summary `rclone serve sftp --auth-proxy` caches the auth proxy's backend keyed on username, credential and client IP, not the authentication method, so a cache hit skips the proxy. The cached public-key credential is the base64 public key, not a secret, so an attacker who knows it sends it as a password and gets the victim's read-write VFS. `PasswordCallback` is unconditional, so key-only deployments cannot disable the password path. ### Details `cmd/serve/proxy/proxy.go` `generateCacheKey` omits `authKind` from the key: ```go func generateCacheKey(user, auth, clientIP string) string { mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, cacheKeyHMACKey) mac.Write([]byte(auth)) // Separate the two so ('ab', 'c') can't collide with ('a', 'bc') mac.Write([]byte{0}) mac.Write([]byte(clientIP)) return user + '-' + hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil)[:8]) } ``` `Proxy.Call` reads `isPublicKey` only on a cache miss, so a hit skips the proxy: ```go clientIP := ipFromAddr(remoteAddr) // Cache key includes the auth and the client IP so credential or // address changes don't hit a stale entry cacheKey := generateCacheKey(user, auth, clientIP) // Look in the cache first with the credential-aware key value, ok := p.vfsCache.GetMaybe(cacheKey) // If not found then call the proxy for a fresh answer if !ok { kind := authPassword if isPublicKey { kind = authPublicKey } value, err = p.call(user, auth, kind, clientIP) ``` The only remaining guard checks the credential, not the method: ```go authHash := sha256.Sum256([]byte(auth)) if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(authHash[:], entry.pwHash[:]) != 1 { ``` `cmd/serve/sftp/server.go` `PublicKeyCallback`: ```go _, vfsKey, err := s.provider.Proxy().Call( c.User(), base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(pubKey.Marshal()), true, c.RemoteAddr().String(), ) ``` and `PasswordCallback` (the public key is a public `authorized_keys` field, sent verbatim as the password): ```go _, vfsKey, err := s.provider.Proxy().Call(c.User(), string(pass), false, c.RemoteAddr().String()) ``` ### PoC 1. Run an auth proxy that accepts public keys and refuses every password, so any password success proves the proxy was skipped rather than persuaded. 2. Start `rclone serve sftp --auth-proxy <that program>`. 3. Negative control: a password login on a cold cache is refused at the SSH handshake. 4. The victim logs in with their private key, then may disconnect. 5. Within the cache lifetime, from the same client IP, the attacker opens an SSH session as the same username using password authentication, with the password set to the victim's base64 public key. 6. The attacker is authenticated and receives the victim's VFS. Verified end to end against a real `rclone serve sftp` listener on `127.0.0.1`: holding only the base64 public key, the attacker read the victim's file and wrote a new file into the victim's backend. The proxy refuses every password, so the attacker's success proves it was never consulted; an instrumented proxy separately recorded zero invocations during the attacker's call. Self-contained Go tests at package level and over SSH, plus a patch, are available on request. ### Preconditions - `serve sftp` with `--auth-proxy`, the only affected server: `serve ftp`, `http` and `webdav` pass `isPublicKey=false`, `serve s3` uses only `CallAccessKey`. - The proxy treats the methods differently, the sharp case a key-only policy. - The victim's key entry is still cached; default lifetime is 300 seconds of disuse refreshed on each access, so the session need not stay open. - Same username. - Same client IP; on a unix socket `ipFromAddr` returns `''` and this vanishes. ### Impact Authentication bypass: with only the victim's public SSH key an attacker gains read and write access to the backend without the proxy being called. The shared-IP precondition is weak behind NAT, a bastion, a load balancer or a unix socket. ### Suggested fix Add the auth kind to the cache key HMAC and check it on a hit, as with the client-IP fix before it. A v1.75.1 patch, with a regression assertion in `TestRun/CacheKey`, refuses the attack and leaves the proxy and sftp suites passing. ### Relationship to the 2026-09-04 advisories A sibling of that batch, not a duplicate. CVE-2026-88017 added the client IP (hence `clientIP` in `generateCacheKey`) but not the auth kind, which is this issue; CVE-2026-88018 and CVE-2026-88044 cover different entry points. ### Version Reproduced on v1.75.1; `proxy.go` and `sftp/server.go` on `master` at commit 1c3e432c3fdbf98c5800c0390496d6944bac53b0 are byte-identical to the release.

GHSA-f8p4-8g4j-q3m2.title: Unauthenticated oversized RC JSON requests exhaust server memory before authorization
GHSA-f8p4-8g4j-q3m2.description: ### Summary When rclone's remote control (RC) server is enabled without HTTP authentication, a client with access to its listening port can exhaust the process's available memory by sending a large JSON POST to an RC method the client is not authorized to invoke. The server decodes the JSON body **before** checking the method's authorization requirement and subsequently includes the supplied input in the error response. Under a constrained memory budget this can terminate rclone. The protected operation is rejected and never executed: the observed impact is denial of service, not an authorization bypass. ### Details In `fs/rc/rcserver/rcserver.go`, `(*Server).handlePost` on the tested development revision: 1. Calls `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&in)` at line 227 without enforcing a request-body size limit. 2. Looks up the RC method at line 245. 3. Checks whether it requires authorization at lines 251-255. 4. On denial, invokes `writeError` with the already decoded input. `fs/rc/params.go:313-327` incorporates that input into the error object, causing further encoding and response-processing costs. The authorization decision is therefore too late to prevent resource consumption from the incoming body. A small request to the protected method normally receives HTTP `403 Forbidden`. The attacker must be able to connect to an RC listener **without configured HTTP authentication**. The RC interface normally binds to loopback (`localhost:5572`), so an off-host attacker requires an exposed or forwarded listener. Loopback-only binding does not prevent other local Linux users from accessing the service: an unprivileged UID 65534 client was separately observed terminating a root-owned rclone process. A finite service memory budget is necessary for the demonstrated OOM termination; thresholds depend on runtime configuration. The finding does not demonstrate a bypass of configured HTTP Basic Auth. The tested source revision is 81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3 (development v1.76.0). The official published releases v1.46 (tag v1.46.0), v1.74.4 and v1.75.2 were reproduced independently. The precise first affected version and any fixed release remain unknown; not every intermediate release was experimentally tested. ### Proof of concept The following example uses the tested modern RC endpoint and a 192 MiB service memory limit. Start the real rclone executable inside the VM: ```bash systemd-run --unit=rclone-rc-repro \ -p MemoryMax=192M -p TasksMax=80 -- \ /path/to/rclone rcd --rc-addr 127.0.0.1:5572 ``` Verify that the protected method is denied without credentials: ```bash curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{}' http://127.0.0.1:5572/core/gc # Expected: 403 ``` Send one bounded JSON body to the same protected method: ```python import http.client body = b'{'payload':['' + b'A' * (48 * 1024 * 1024) + b'']}' conn = http.client.HTTPConnection('127.0.0.1', 5572, timeout=15) try: conn.request( 'POST', '/core/gc', body=body, headers={'Content-Type': 'application/json'}, ) print(conn.getresponse().status) except (OSError, http.client.HTTPException) as exc: print(type(exc).__name__, str(exc)) finally: conn.close() ``` Check the service's termination result: ```bash systemctl show rclone-rc-repro.service \ -p ActiveState -p Result -p ExecMainStatus ``` **Expected:** Denied methods do not consume or retain unbounded request bodies; the service remains available. **Observed:** In the tested constrained setup, the client was disconnected and the rclone process ended with `Result=oom-kill` and `ExecMainStatus=9`. The protected operation was not executed. For the historical `v1.46` release, the expressly protected test method is `rc/noopauth` rather than `core/gc`. ### Impact An attacker able to access RC without HTTP authentication can kill a memory-constrained rclone process, interrupting active transfers and other services within the same process. This is reproducible from another low-privilege local account when the RC listener uses its default loopback binding, or remotely if the listener is made accessible to an untrusted network. **Mitigation:** Enable RC HTTP authentication and restrict access to trusted clients. Treat loopback binding as a network exposure control, **not** an operating-system-user isolation boundary. If the RC interface is accessed through a trusted reverse proxy, set a request-body limit and prevent direct bypass of that proxy. **Recommended fix:** 1. Resolve the target method and enforce its authorization requirement **before** parsing request bodies. 2. Enforce a bounded request-body size on all RC endpoints, including intentionally unauthenticated endpoints; reject oversized requests with HTTP `413 Request Entity Too Large`. 3. Do not reflect arbitrarily large attacker-controlled input in error responses. 4. Add regression tests for protected methods with large bodies, size-limit enforcement on public endpoints, and ordinary authorized requests.

GHSA-hwj7-wp9g-wrv9.title: Rclone --htpasswd leaks valid usernames through a bcrypt timing oracle
GHSA-hwj7-wp9g-wrv9.description: ### Summary Rclone's shared HTTP authentication middleware returns immediately when an HTTP Basic Auth username is absent from the configured htpasswd file, but performs password-hash verification when the username exists. With the bcrypt hashes recommended by Rclone's documentation, both paths return the same HTTP 401 response yet differ by roughly 100 ms. An unauthenticated remote client can enumerate valid usernames using ordinary Basic Auth requests with an incorrect password. Official rclone v1.75.2 produced a 38.7x median separation (2.68 ms absent versus 103.51 ms existing bcrypt user); the exported middleware produced 106.2x. Suggested Moderate, CWE-208, CVSS 5.3. ### Details ## Affected configuration and attack surface Confirmed for Rclone HTTP listeners using an htpasswd file containing bcrypt hashes, including serve http, serve webdav, serve restic, serve s3, rcd with --rc-htpasswd, and metrics with --metrics-htpasswd. The listener must be reachable. No valid credentials, user interaction, malformed traffic, concurrency, or high request rate is required. ## Root cause Rclone constructs its htpasswd authentication middleware in lib/http/middleware.go using github.com/abbot/go-http-auth v0.4.0. In BasicAuth.CheckAuth, the dependency looks up the candidate username and returns immediately if the provider returns an empty secret: ```go secret := a.Secrets(user, a.Realm) if secret == '' { return '' } // existing user continues to the selected password hash verifier if compare([]byte(secret), []byte(password)) != nil { return '' } ``` For an absent username, no hash is evaluated. For a present bcrypt username, bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword runs before the same 401 failure response. Rclone documentation supports MD5, SHA1 and bcrypt htpasswd entries and recommends bcrypt. Relevant source: - Rclone middleware: https://github.com/rclone/rclone/blob/81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3/lib/http/middleware.go#L94-L99 - Rclone middleware call and 401 path: https://github.com/rclone/rclone/blob/81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3/lib/http/middleware.go#L42-L68 - Dependency short-circuit: https://github.com/abbot/go-http-auth/blob/v0.4.0/basic.go#L83-L95 - Rclone bcrypt recommendation: https://github.com/rclone/rclone/blob/81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3/docs/content/commands/rclone_serve_http.md#L158-L166 ## Affected versions The vulnerable middleware was introduced by commit 4ad62ec0166300a5d96a459bcd1c3b742a554ddf on 2021-04-19. The first containing release is v1.56.0. Confirmed affected through stable v1.75.2 and current master commit 81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3. No patched version was identified as of 2026-10-25. ## Duplicate review I reviewed all 44 public Rclone GitHub Security Advisories for timing, username, enumeration, bcrypt, htpasswd, and Basic Auth references. None describes this oracle. I also searched Rclone issues and abbot/go-http-auth issues. Rclone #7892 documents bcrypt performance overhead but not the missing-user short-circuit or username enumeration. abbot/go-http-auth#14 is a general constant-time concern, not this username-dependent hash-work discrepancy. ## Remediation guidance Failure paths should perform equivalent password-hash work regardless of whether a username exists. For bcrypt, verify against a stable dummy hash with the deployment-matched work factor when the provider does not find the username. Because htpasswd files can mix algorithms and bcrypt costs, a complete design should enforce/normalize one algorithm and cost or otherwise avoid revealing hash class/work factor. Rate limiting and failed-auth backoff are defense in depth only. Regression tests should instrument the verifier and assert equivalent work for absent usernames and existing users with a wrong password. ## CVE request and disclosure Please assess whether this confirmed network-reachable authentication-boundary issue warrants a GitHub Security Advisory and CVE assignment. I defer final severity, CWE, CVSS, and CVE decisions to the maintainers and would appreciate reporter credit under this GitHub account. All testing used loopback listeners and local files. No third-party host, account, credential, or data was accessed. AI assistance was used for source review and report preparation; I verified the issue with the checksummed official release binary, an independent standard-library client, and the exported Rclone middleware. ### Proof of concept ## 1. Prepare a bcrypt htpasswd entry From an Rclone checkout: ```sh mkdir -p /tmp/rclone-timing-root cp lib/http/testdata/.htpasswd /tmp/rclone-timing-htpasswd ``` The fixture contains a cost-10 bcrypt account named bcrypt. Alternatively use htpasswd -cB as recommended by the Rclone documentation. ## 2. Start Rclone on loopback ```sh rclone serve http /tmp/rclone-timing-root \ --htpasswd /tmp/rclone-timing-htpasswd \ --addr 127.0.0.1:18092 \ --config '' ``` ## 3. Sequential standard-library client ```python import base64, hashlib, json, statistics, time import urllib.error, urllib.request URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:18092/' WRONG_PASSWORD = 'definitely-wrong-password' def probe(username): token = base64.b64encode(f'{username}:{WRONG_PASSWORD}'.encode()).decode() req = urllib.request.Request(URL, headers={'Authorization': f'Basic {token}'}) started = time.perf_counter_ns() try: response = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) except urllib.error.HTTPError as error: response = error elapsed_ms = (time.perf_counter_ns() - started) / 1_000_000 body = response.read() fingerprint = { 'status': response.status, 'body_sha256': hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest(), 'www_authenticate': response.headers.get('WWW-Authenticate'), 'content_type': response.headers.get('Content-Type'), } return elapsed_ms, fingerprint for _ in range(3): probe('missing-user') probe('bcrypt') unknown, existing = [], [] for index in range(20): elapsed, unknown_response = probe(f'missing-user-{index:02d}') unknown.append(elapsed) elapsed, existing_response = probe('bcrypt') existing.append(elapsed) unknown_median = statistics.median(unknown) existing_median = statistics.median(existing) print(json.dumps({ 'requests_per_class': 20, 'unknown_user_median_ms': unknown_median, 'existing_user_median_ms': existing_median, 'median_separation_ratio': existing_median / unknown_median, 'responses_identical_excluding_timing': unknown_response == existing_response, 'response': unknown_response, }, indent=2)) ``` Observed against the official rclone-v1.75.2-windows-amd64.zip, whose SHA-256 8a9db2bad1dc79a65b3348fd857069598e2aab7cf4d118b77b1df23055aff818 matched Rclone's SHA256SUMS: ```json { 'requests_per_class': 20, 'unknown_user_median_ms': 2.67555, 'existing_user_median_ms': 103.511, 'median_separation_ratio': 38.687746444656234, 'responses_identical_excluding_timing': true, 'response': { 'status': 401, 'body_sha256': 'eea3a195b4f27ccc15681ea830d68d719afb5d417d16e1a174b7d3b3b9e14af4', 'www_authenticate': 'Basic realm=\'\'', 'content_type': 'text/plain' } } ``` A direct loopback httptest server wrapped with exported rclone/lib/http.MiddlewareAuthHtpasswd independently produced absent-user median 1.0069 ms, existing-user median 106.9457 ms, 106.21x separation, and identical non-timing response observables. ### Impact An unauthenticated attacker who can reach an Rclone listener protected with --htpasswd can distinguish valid and invalid usernames. This enables discovery of administrative, service, customer, or tenant account names; focusing password guessing or credential stuffing on known accounts; and targeted phishing using confirmed identifiers. It does not by itself reveal a password or grant authentication. The signal is strongest in Rclone's recommended bcrypt configuration because the missing-user path skips about 100 ms of deliberate work.

GHSA-m97j-7x65-wh93.title: rclone swift, netstorage and seafile backends leak credentials on cross-host or HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects
GHSA-m97j-7x65-wh93.description: ### Summary rclone follows HTTP redirects with Go's default redirect policy unless a backend installs its own. That policy copies every request header onto the next hop except `Authorization`, `WWW-Authenticate`, `Cookie` and `Cookie2`. It drops those few only when the hostname changes, and it never looks at the scheme. Several backends send their credentials in custom headers, or in an `Authorization` header that a same-host HTTPS to HTTP redirect keeps. In those backends a redirect from the configured endpoint sent the credentials to another host, or over plaintext HTTP, or both. This advisory covers three backends: | Backend | What leaked | Redirect which leaks it | Affected since | |---|---|---|---| | `swift` | Session token in `X-Auth-Token` on every storage request. v1 auth: user name and API key in `X-Auth-User` / `X-Auth-Key`. v2/v3 auth: the password or application credential secret in the JSON request body, resent on a 307/308. | Cross-host and HTTPS to HTTP | every release | | `netstorage` | Account name and request signature in `X-Akamai-ACS-Auth-Data` / `X-Akamai-ACS-Auth-Sign`, plus `X-Akamai-ACS-Action` | Cross-host and HTTPS to HTTP | v1.58.0 | | `seafile` | API token in `Authorization: Token ...`, and the account password while logging in, including the two-factor step of `rclone config` | Same-host HTTPS to HTTP | v1.52.0 | rclone v1.76.0 fixes each backend. It also adds a general protection: rclone's HTTP transport now refuses to follow any HTTPS to HTTP redirect. ### Details **swift.** The `github.com/ncw/swift/v2` library builds its own unexported `http.Client` with no redirect policy, and rclone can only supply its `Transport`. So rclone had no way to stop the library forwarding `X-Auth-Token`, `X-Auth-User` or `X-Auth-Key` to whatever host a redirect pointed at, over any scheme. For v2 and v3 authentication the password is posted in a rewindable JSON body, which net/http resends on a 307 or 308 redirect to another host. **netstorage.** The client had no redirect policy. The signer sets the authentication headers on every request, so they were copied onto every redirect hop. The signature is an HMAC-SHA256 bound to one path and action, within Akamai's time window. The G2O key cannot be recovered from it, but someone who captures it can replay that exact request within the window. **seafile.** The API client and the two-factor configuration client had no redirect policy. For other hostnames Go already drops `Authorization`, but it keeps it on a redirect to the same hostname whatever the scheme. A redirect from `https://` to `http://` on the same host therefore sent the API token in cleartext. A 307 or 308 downgrade during login resent the password in cleartext too. All three need the configured endpoint, or something in front of it that holds a valid certificate for it (a proxy, load balancer or CDN), to issue the redirect. A passive network attacker cannot inject a redirect into an HTTPS session. What they gain is the ability to read the credentials once the endpoint has sent them over plaintext HTTP, or once it has sent them to a host it was never trusted with. ### Impact - **swift:** whoever receives the token can list, read, write and delete objects in the whole account until the token expires. The v1 API key and the v2/v3 password are long-lived credentials. - **seafile:** the API token gives full access to the account. The password can be used to log in. - **netstorage:** whoever receives the signature can replay the one signed request within the time window. ### Patches Fixed in rclone v1.76.0: - `fshttp`: rclone's HTTP transport refuses to follow a redirect from `https://` to `http://` and returns an error naming the new `--allow-https-downgrade` flag. Because the check is in the transport, it also covers clients that libraries build for themselves, such as the swift library's. Use `--allow-https-downgrade` to follow such redirects, for example when downloading from a mirror which redirects to plain HTTP. **This is a behaviour change:** the `http` backend and `rclone copyurl` used to follow these redirects silently. - `swift`: the transport rclone gives the library removes `X-Auth-Token`, `X-Auth-User` and `X-Auth-Key` once a redirect leaves the original host and port. It refuses an HTTPS to HTTP redirect, and a cross-host redirect which would resend the request body. - `netstorage`: the three `X-Akamai-ACS-*` headers are removed once a redirect leaves the original host and port, and HTTPS to HTTP redirects are refused. - `seafile`: HTTPS to HTTP redirects are refused for the API client and the configuration client. The swift, netstorage and seafile backends refuse a downgrade even when `--allow-https-downgrade` is set, because following it would send their credentials in cleartext. ### Workarounds Before upgrading, only use endpoints you trust not to redirect elsewhere. For swift that includes the storage URL returned by the auth server. Prior to 1.75.1, rclone core does not reject parent-directory segments in source Object.Remote() values before fs/list, fs/walk, fs/sync, and fs/operations pass those values to destination backends. A flat-keyspace source object store populated with native non-rclone tooling can contain a raw .. key segment, and affected b2, swift, qingstor, oracleobjectstorage, internetarchive, smb, storj, sftp, webdav, ftp, filelu, shade, and sia destinations use path.Join(root, remote) before EncodeDot can neutralize the segment. A copy or upload can therefore escape the configured root into another bucket, share, or path reachable by the victim credential, with sftp and smb potentially reaching other filesystem or share locations under the same login authority. This issue is fixed in version 1.75.1.

CVE-2026-93986.title: rclone before 1.75.1 fails to confine names from server and third ...
CVE-2026-93986.description: rclone before 1.75.1 fails to confine names from server and third-party listing responses to the listed directory, allowing path traversal sequences in object names. Attackers can craft special names containing forward slashes and parent directory references to potentially write outside the destination root, though downstream protections in the local backend currently block actual file escape.

CVE-2026-93987.title: rclone versions 1.56.0 through 1.75.0 contain a path traversal vu ...
CVE-2026-93987.description: rclone versions 1.56.0 through 1.75.0 contain a path traversal vulnerability in the `rclone serve docker` volume plugin. newVolume() in cmd/serve/docker/volume.go computes a volume's mountpoint as filepath.Join(drv.root, name) from the attacker-supplied `name` field of a Docker VolumeDriver.Create request without verifying that the result stays within drv.root (default /var/lib/docker-volumes/rclone), and checkMountpoint() then creates that directory with file.MkdirAll before mounting. A volume name containing enough `..` components (e.g. "../../../../../../etc") therefore resolves outside the base directory, allowing anyone able to submit a VolumeDriver.Create request to the plugin socket — normally the Docker daemon, or a workload that can request named volumes in a multi-tenant orchestration setup — to make the privileged rclone plugin process create a directory and mount a remote filesystem specified in the same request at an arbitrary host path, shadowing or disrupting system directories. The advisory notes Volume.restoreState() had the same missing validation when reloading persisted volume state. Fixed in 1.75.1.

GHSA-3xpx-hjg2-vrjh.title: rclone Ulozto backend leaks auth tokens (X-Auth-Token, X-User-Token) on redirect via wrong client
GHSA-3xpx-hjg2-vrjh.description: ## Summary The rclone Ulozto backend leaks persistent authentication tokens (X-Auth-Token, X-User-Token) to unintended hosts on HTTP redirect. The download path incorrectly uses the auth-bearing f.rest client to fetch from server-provided CDN URLs, instead of using the purpose-built unauthenticated f.cdn client. ## Root Cause The Ulozto backend creates two rest clients at ulozto.go:128-135: f.cdn (unauthenticated) and f.rest (carries X-Auth-Token and X-User-Token). The upload path correctly uses f.cdn (ulozto.go:396), but the download path in (*Object).Open at ulozto.go:838 uses o.fs.rest.Call, sending auth tokens to CDN infrastructure unnecessarily. The HTTP client from fshttp.NewClient(ctx) has no CheckRedirect. Go's shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect only strips Authorization/Cookie. ```text - (*Object).Open at backend/ulozto/ulozto.go:838 uses f.rest instead of f.cdn for CDN downloads - f.rest.SetHeader('X-Auth-Token', ...) at ulozto.go:144 sets persistent app API key - f.rest.SetHeader('X-User-Token', ...) at ulozto.go:274 sets persistent session token - fshttp.NewClientCustom at fs/fshttp/http.go:318-326 creates client with no CheckRedirect ``` ## Impact An attacker who can observe CDN redirect traffic captures the victim's Ulozto credentials. X-Auth-Token is a long-lived app API key granting persistent API access to the entire account. X-User-Token is a session token granting session-level access. Together they enable read, modify, and manage operations. The API endpoint is hardcoded to https://apis.uloz.to with no HTTP option, constraining the attack to CDN redirect interception (AC:H). ## Proof of Concept ```text Dependencies: Go 1.21+, rclone source tree ``` ```go cdn := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { http.Redirect(w, r, targetURL+r.URL.Path, http.StatusTemporaryRedirect) })) target := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { capturedAuthToken = r.Header.Get('X-Auth-Token') capturedUserToken = r.Header.Get('X-User-Token') })) req.Header.Set('X-Auth-Token', 'test-app-token-12345') req.Header.Set('X-User-Token', 'test-user-session-token') client := &http.Client{} client.Do(req) ``` ```text Both X-Auth-Token and X-User-Token are forwarded to the redirect target. ``` ## Attack Chain 1. **Exposure:** The Ulozto backend ships in every rclone binary, activated with type = ulozto. Downloads trigger (*Object).Open. 2. **Control:** Attacker controls a network position (DNS/BGP hijack, compromised CDN edge) to observe CDN traffic. 3. **Path:** (*Object).Open gets CDN URL from API (ulozto.go:819), fetches via o.fs.rest.Call (ulozto.go:838). rest.Call copies persistent headers (X-Auth-Token, X-User-Token) at rest.go:377 and dispatches via c.Do(req) at rest.go:440. 4. **Guard:** Go's shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect only strips Authorization/Cookie. Transport's redirectLeavesHost only strips --header values. No guard for X-Auth-Token or X-User-Token. 5. **Primitive:** Redirect target receives the long-lived app API key and session token. 6. **Result:** Attacker gains persistent API access and session-level account access to the victim's Ulozto storage. ## Bypass Evidence No prior fix or guard exists. f.cdn was created at ulozto.go:134 specifically for unauthenticated CDN operations and is correctly used for uploads (ulozto.go:396). The download path incorrectly uses f.rest. The rest.Opts provides NoRedirect, CheckRedirect, AuthRedirect fields the download path does not use. The codebase recognizes X-Auth-Token as sensitive for logging (http.go:438-441) but only for debug output, not redirect protection. The hardcoded HTTPS endpoint constrains but does not eliminate the attack surface. ## Affected Versions - Ecosystem: Go - Package: github.com/rclone/rclone - Confirmed affected range: <= 1.75.1 - Latest release checked: v1.75.1 (Go module proxy, 2026-09-04) - Fix status: not fixed The vulnerability exists since the Ulozto backend was first added. No fix exists in any version. ## Suggested Fix Switch the download request at ulozto.go:838 from o.fs.rest.Call to o.fs.cdn.Call. The f.cdn client carries no auth headers and was created for exactly this purpose, consistent with the upload path (ulozto.go:396). Additionally, implement a CheckRedirect function to strip X-Auth-Token and X-User-Token on cross-host redirects and block HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrades. No interim mitigation is available. Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

GHSA-66qv-66mg-9h74.title: serve sftp: auth-proxy cache key omits the credential kind, letting a public key be replayed as a password
GHSA-66qv-66mg-9h74.description: ### Summary `rclone serve sftp --auth-proxy` caches the auth proxy's backend keyed on username, credential and client IP, not the authentication method, so a cache hit skips the proxy. The cached public-key credential is the base64 public key, not a secret, so an attacker who knows it sends it as a password and gets the victim's read-write VFS. `PasswordCallback` is unconditional, so key-only deployments cannot disable the password path. ### Details `cmd/serve/proxy/proxy.go` `generateCacheKey` omits `authKind` from the key: ```go func generateCacheKey(user, auth, clientIP string) string { mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, cacheKeyHMACKey) mac.Write([]byte(auth)) // Separate the two so ('ab', 'c') can't collide with ('a', 'bc') mac.Write([]byte{0}) mac.Write([]byte(clientIP)) return user + '-' + hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil)[:8]) } ``` `Proxy.Call` reads `isPublicKey` only on a cache miss, so a hit skips the proxy: ```go clientIP := ipFromAddr(remoteAddr) // Cache key includes the auth and the client IP so credential or // address changes don't hit a stale entry cacheKey := generateCacheKey(user, auth, clientIP) // Look in the cache first with the credential-aware key value, ok := p.vfsCache.GetMaybe(cacheKey) // If not found then call the proxy for a fresh answer if !ok { kind := authPassword if isPublicKey { kind = authPublicKey } value, err = p.call(user, auth, kind, clientIP) ``` The only remaining guard checks the credential, not the method: ```go authHash := sha256.Sum256([]byte(auth)) if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(authHash[:], entry.pwHash[:]) != 1 { ``` `cmd/serve/sftp/server.go` `PublicKeyCallback`: ```go _, vfsKey, err := s.provider.Proxy().Call( c.User(), base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(pubKey.Marshal()), true, c.RemoteAddr().String(), ) ``` and `PasswordCallback` (the public key is a public `authorized_keys` field, sent verbatim as the password): ```go _, vfsKey, err := s.provider.Proxy().Call(c.User(), string(pass), false, c.RemoteAddr().String()) ``` ### PoC 1. Run an auth proxy that accepts public keys and refuses every password, so any password success proves the proxy was skipped rather than persuaded. 2. Start `rclone serve sftp --auth-proxy <that program>`. 3. Negative control: a password login on a cold cache is refused at the SSH handshake. 4. The victim logs in with their private key, then may disconnect. 5. Within the cache lifetime, from the same client IP, the attacker opens an SSH session as the same username using password authentication, with the password set to the victim's base64 public key. 6. The attacker is authenticated and receives the victim's VFS. Verified end to end against a real `rclone serve sftp` listener on `127.0.0.1`: holding only the base64 public key, the attacker read the victim's file and wrote a new file into the victim's backend. The proxy refuses every password, so the attacker's success proves it was never consulted; an instrumented proxy separately recorded zero invocations during the attacker's call. Self-contained Go tests at package level and over SSH, plus a patch, are available on request. ### Preconditions - `serve sftp` with `--auth-proxy`, the only affected server: `serve ftp`, `http` and `webdav` pass `isPublicKey=false`, `serve s3` uses only `CallAccessKey`. - The proxy treats the methods differently, the sharp case a key-only policy. - The victim's key entry is still cached; default lifetime is 300 seconds of disuse refreshed on each access, so the session need not stay open. - Same username. - Same client IP; on a unix socket `ipFromAddr` returns `''` and this vanishes. ### Impact Authentication bypass: with only the victim's public SSH key an attacker gains read and write access to the backend without the proxy being called. The shared-IP precondition is weak behind NAT, a bastion, a load balancer or a unix socket. ### Suggested fix Add the auth kind to the cache key HMAC and check it on a hit, as with the client-IP fix before it. A v1.75.1 patch, with a regression assertion in `TestRun/CacheKey`, refuses the attack and leaves the proxy and sftp suites passing. ### Relationship to the 2026-09-04 advisories A sibling of that batch, not a duplicate. CVE-2026-88017 added the client IP (hence `clientIP` in `generateCacheKey`) but not the auth kind, which is this issue; CVE-2026-88018 and CVE-2026-88044 cover different entry points. ### Version Reproduced on v1.75.1; `proxy.go` and `sftp/server.go` on `master` at commit 1c3e432c3fdbf98c5800c0390496d6944bac53b0 are byte-identical to the release.

GHSA-f8p4-8g4j-q3m2.title: Unauthenticated oversized RC JSON requests exhaust server memory before authorization
GHSA-f8p4-8g4j-q3m2.description: ### Summary When rclone's remote control (RC) server is enabled without HTTP authentication, a client with access to its listening port can exhaust the process's available memory by sending a large JSON POST to an RC method the client is not authorized to invoke. The server decodes the JSON body **before** checking the method's authorization requirement and subsequently includes the supplied input in the error response. Under a constrained memory budget this can terminate rclone. The protected operation is rejected and never executed: the observed impact is denial of service, not an authorization bypass. ### Details In `fs/rc/rcserver/rcserver.go`, `(*Server).handlePost` on the tested development revision: 1. Calls `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&in)` at line 227 without enforcing a request-body size limit. 2. Looks up the RC method at line 245. 3. Checks whether it requires authorization at lines 251-255. 4. On denial, invokes `writeError` with the already decoded input. `fs/rc/params.go:313-327` incorporates that input into the error object, causing further encoding and response-processing costs. The authorization decision is therefore too late to prevent resource consumption from the incoming body. A small request to the protected method normally receives HTTP `403 Forbidden`. The attacker must be able to connect to an RC listener **without configured HTTP authentication**. The RC interface normally binds to loopback (`localhost:5572`), so an off-host attacker requires an exposed or forwarded listener. Loopback-only binding does not prevent other local Linux users from accessing the service: an unprivileged UID 65534 client was separately observed terminating a root-owned rclone process. A finite service memory budget is necessary for the demonstrated OOM termination; thresholds depend on runtime configuration. The finding does not demonstrate a bypass of configured HTTP Basic Auth. The tested source revision is 81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3 (development v1.76.0). The official published releases v1.46 (tag v1.46.0), v1.74.4 and v1.75.2 were reproduced independently. The precise first affected version and any fixed release remain unknown; not every intermediate release was experimentally tested. ### Proof of concept The following example uses the tested modern RC endpoint and a 192 MiB service memory limit. Start the real rclone executable inside the VM: ```bash systemd-run --unit=rclone-rc-repro \ -p MemoryMax=192M -p TasksMax=80 -- \ /path/to/rclone rcd --rc-addr 127.0.0.1:5572 ``` Verify that the protected method is denied without credentials: ```bash curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{}' http://127.0.0.1:5572/core/gc # Expected: 403 ``` Send one bounded JSON body to the same protected method: ```python import http.client body = b'{'payload':['' + b'A' * (48 * 1024 * 1024) + b'']}' conn = http.client.HTTPConnection('127.0.0.1', 5572, timeout=15) try: conn.request( 'POST', '/core/gc', body=body, headers={'Content-Type': 'application/json'}, ) print(conn.getresponse().status) except (OSError, http.client.HTTPException) as exc: print(type(exc).__name__, str(exc)) finally: conn.close() ``` Check the service's termination result: ```bash systemctl show rclone-rc-repro.service \ -p ActiveState -p Result -p ExecMainStatus ``` **Expected:** Denied methods do not consume or retain unbounded request bodies; the service remains available. **Observed:** In the tested constrained setup, the client was disconnected and the rclone process ended with `Result=oom-kill` and `ExecMainStatus=9`. The protected operation was not executed. For the historical `v1.46` release, the expressly protected test method is `rc/noopauth` rather than `core/gc`. ### Impact An attacker able to access RC without HTTP authentication can kill a memory-constrained rclone process, interrupting active transfers and other services within the same process. This is reproducible from another low-privilege local account when the RC listener uses its default loopback binding, or remotely if the listener is made accessible to an untrusted network. **Mitigation:** Enable RC HTTP authentication and restrict access to trusted clients. Treat loopback binding as a network exposure control, **not** an operating-system-user isolation boundary. If the RC interface is accessed through a trusted reverse proxy, set a request-body limit and prevent direct bypass of that proxy. **Recommended fix:** 1. Resolve the target method and enforce its authorization requirement **before** parsing request bodies. 2. Enforce a bounded request-body size on all RC endpoints, including intentionally unauthenticated endpoints; reject oversized requests with HTTP `413 Request Entity Too Large`. 3. Do not reflect arbitrarily large attacker-controlled input in error responses. 4. Add regression tests for protected methods with large bodies, size-limit enforcement on public endpoints, and ordinary authorized requests.

GHSA-hwj7-wp9g-wrv9.title: Rclone --htpasswd leaks valid usernames through a bcrypt timing oracle
GHSA-hwj7-wp9g-wrv9.description: ### Summary Rclone's shared HTTP authentication middleware returns immediately when an HTTP Basic Auth username is absent from the configured htpasswd file, but performs password-hash verification when the username exists. With the bcrypt hashes recommended by Rclone's documentation, both paths return the same HTTP 401 response yet differ by roughly 100 ms. An unauthenticated remote client can enumerate valid usernames using ordinary Basic Auth requests with an incorrect password. Official rclone v1.75.2 produced a 38.7x median separation (2.68 ms absent versus 103.51 ms existing bcrypt user); the exported middleware produced 106.2x. Suggested Moderate, CWE-208, CVSS 5.3. ### Details ## Affected configuration and attack surface Confirmed for Rclone HTTP listeners using an htpasswd file containing bcrypt hashes, including serve http, serve webdav, serve restic, serve s3, rcd with --rc-htpasswd, and metrics with --metrics-htpasswd. The listener must be reachable. No valid credentials, user interaction, malformed traffic, concurrency, or high request rate is required. ## Root cause Rclone constructs its htpasswd authentication middleware in lib/http/middleware.go using github.com/abbot/go-http-auth v0.4.0. In BasicAuth.CheckAuth, the dependency looks up the candidate username and returns immediately if the provider returns an empty secret: ```go secret := a.Secrets(user, a.Realm) if secret == '' { return '' } // existing user continues to the selected password hash verifier if compare([]byte(secret), []byte(password)) != nil { return '' } ``` For an absent username, no hash is evaluated. For a present bcrypt username, bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword runs before the same 401 failure response. Rclone documentation supports MD5, SHA1 and bcrypt htpasswd entries and recommends bcrypt. Relevant source: - Rclone middleware: https://github.com/rclone/rclone/blob/81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3/lib/http/middleware.go#L94-L99 - Rclone middleware call and 401 path: https://github.com/rclone/rclone/blob/81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3/lib/http/middleware.go#L42-L68 - Dependency short-circuit: https://github.com/abbot/go-http-auth/blob/v0.4.0/basic.go#L83-L95 - Rclone bcrypt recommendation: https://github.com/rclone/rclone/blob/81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3/docs/content/commands/rclone_serve_http.md#L158-L166 ## Affected versions The vulnerable middleware was introduced by commit 4ad62ec0166300a5d96a459bcd1c3b742a554ddf on 2021-04-19. The first containing release is v1.56.0. Confirmed affected through stable v1.75.2 and current master commit 81e7372f6fbedfa80592e9a564593d63a8dc32f3. No patched version was identified as of 2026-10-25. ## Duplicate review I reviewed all 44 public Rclone GitHub Security Advisories for timing, username, enumeration, bcrypt, htpasswd, and Basic Auth references. None describes this oracle. I also searched Rclone issues and abbot/go-http-auth issues. Rclone #7892 documents bcrypt performance overhead but not the missing-user short-circuit or username enumeration. abbot/go-http-auth#14 is a general constant-time concern, not this username-dependent hash-work discrepancy. ## Remediation guidance Failure paths should perform equivalent password-hash work regardless of whether a username exists. For bcrypt, verify against a stable dummy hash with the deployment-matched work factor when the provider does not find the username. Because htpasswd files can mix algorithms and bcrypt costs, a complete design should enforce/normalize one algorithm and cost or otherwise avoid revealing hash class/work factor. Rate limiting and failed-auth backoff are defense in depth only. Regression tests should instrument the verifier and assert equivalent work for absent usernames and existing users with a wrong password. ## CVE request and disclosure Please assess whether this confirmed network-reachable authentication-boundary issue warrants a GitHub Security Advisory and CVE assignment. I defer final severity, CWE, CVSS, and CVE decisions to the maintainers and would appreciate reporter credit under this GitHub account. All testing used loopback listeners and local files. No third-party host, account, credential, or data was accessed. AI assistance was used for source review and report preparation; I verified the issue with the checksummed official release binary, an independent standard-library client, and the exported Rclone middleware. ### Proof of concept ## 1. Prepare a bcrypt htpasswd entry From an Rclone checkout: ```sh mkdir -p /tmp/rclone-timing-root cp lib/http/testdata/.htpasswd /tmp/rclone-timing-htpasswd ``` The fixture contains a cost-10 bcrypt account named bcrypt. Alternatively use htpasswd -cB as recommended by the Rclone documentation. ## 2. Start Rclone on loopback ```sh rclone serve http /tmp/rclone-timing-root \ --htpasswd /tmp/rclone-timing-htpasswd \ --addr 127.0.0.1:18092 \ --config '' ``` ## 3. Sequential standard-library client ```python import base64, hashlib, json, statistics, time import urllib.error, urllib.request URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:18092/' WRONG_PASSWORD = 'definitely-wrong-password' def probe(username): token = base64.b64encode(f'{username}:{WRONG_PASSWORD}'.encode()).decode() req = urllib.request.Request(URL, headers={'Authorization': f'Basic {token}'}) started = time.perf_counter_ns() try: response = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) except urllib.error.HTTPError as error: response = error elapsed_ms = (time.perf_counter_ns() - started) / 1_000_000 body = response.read() fingerprint = { 'status': response.status, 'body_sha256': hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest(), 'www_authenticate': response.headers.get('WWW-Authenticate'), 'content_type': response.headers.get('Content-Type'), } return elapsed_ms, fingerprint for _ in range(3): probe('missing-user') probe('bcrypt') unknown, existing = [], [] for index in range(20): elapsed, unknown_response = probe(f'missing-user-{index:02d}') unknown.append(elapsed) elapsed, existing_response = probe('bcrypt') existing.append(elapsed) unknown_median = statistics.median(unknown) existing_median = statistics.median(existing) print(json.dumps({ 'requests_per_class': 20, 'unknown_user_median_ms': unknown_median, 'existing_user_median_ms': existing_median, 'median_separation_ratio': existing_median / unknown_median, 'responses_identical_excluding_timing': unknown_response == existing_response, 'response': unknown_response, }, indent=2)) ``` Observed against the official rclone-v1.75.2-windows-amd64.zip, whose SHA-256 8a9db2bad1dc79a65b3348fd857069598e2aab7cf4d118b77b1df23055aff818 matched Rclone's SHA256SUMS: ```json { 'requests_per_class': 20, 'unknown_user_median_ms': 2.67555, 'existing_user_median_ms': 103.511, 'median_separation_ratio': 38.687746444656234, 'responses_identical_excluding_timing': true, 'response': { 'status': 401, 'body_sha256': 'eea3a195b4f27ccc15681ea830d68d719afb5d417d16e1a174b7d3b3b9e14af4', 'www_authenticate': 'Basic realm=\'\'', 'content_type': 'text/plain' } } ``` A direct loopback httptest server wrapped with exported rclone/lib/http.MiddlewareAuthHtpasswd independently produced absent-user median 1.0069 ms, existing-user median 106.9457 ms, 106.21x separation, and identical non-timing response observables. ### Impact An unauthenticated attacker who can reach an Rclone listener protected with --htpasswd can distinguish valid and invalid usernames. This enables discovery of administrative, service, customer, or tenant account names; focusing password guessing or credential stuffing on known accounts; and targeted phishing using confirmed identifiers. It does not by itself reveal a password or grant authentication. The signal is strongest in Rclone's recommended bcrypt configuration because the missing-user path skips about 100 ms of deliberate work.

GHSA-m97j-7x65-wh93.title: rclone swift, netstorage and seafile backends leak credentials on cross-host or HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects
GHSA-m97j-7x65-wh93.description: ### Summary rclone follows HTTP redirects with Go's default redirect policy unless a backend installs its own. That policy copies every request header onto the next hop except `Authorization`, `WWW-Authenticate`, `Cookie` and `Cookie2`. It drops those few only when the hostname changes, and it never looks at the scheme. Several backends send their credentials in custom headers, or in an `Authorization` header that a same-host HTTPS to HTTP redirect keeps. In those backends a redirect from the configured endpoint sent the credentials to another host, or over plaintext HTTP, or both. This advisory covers three backends: | Backend | What leaked | Redirect which leaks it | Affected since | |---|---|---|---| | `swift` | Session token in `X-Auth-Token` on every storage request. v1 auth: user name and API key in `X-Auth-User` / `X-Auth-Key`. v2/v3 auth: the password or application credential secret in the JSON request body, resent on a 307/308. | Cross-host and HTTPS to HTTP | every release | | `netstorage` | Account name and request signature in `X-Akamai-ACS-Auth-Data` / `X-Akamai-ACS-Auth-Sign`, plus `X-Akamai-ACS-Action` | Cross-host and HTTPS to HTTP | v1.58.0 | | `seafile` | API token in `Authorization: Token ...`, and the account password while logging in, including the two-factor step of `rclone config` | Same-host HTTPS to HTTP | v1.52.0 | rclone v1.76.0 fixes each backend. It also adds a general protection: rclone's HTTP transport now refuses to follow any HTTPS to HTTP redirect. ### Details **swift.** The `github.com/ncw/swift/v2` library builds its own unexported `http.Client` with no redirect policy, and rclone can only supply its `Transport`. So rclone had no way to stop the library forwarding `X-Auth-Token`, `X-Auth-User` or `X-Auth-Key` to whatever host a redirect pointed at, over any scheme. For v2 and v3 authentication the password is posted in a rewindable JSON body, which net/http resends on a 307 or 308 redirect to another host. **netstorage.** The client had no redirect policy. The signer sets the authentication headers on every request, so they were copied onto every redirect hop. The signature is an HMAC-SHA256 bound to one path and action, within Akamai's time window. The G2O key cannot be recovered from it, but someone who captures it can replay that exact request within the window. **seafile.** The API client and the two-factor configuration client had no redirect policy. For other hostnames Go already drops `Authorization`, but it keeps it on a redirect to the same hostname whatever the scheme. A redirect from `https://` to `http://` on the same host therefore sent the API token in cleartext. A 307 or 308 downgrade during login resent the password in cleartext too. All three need the configured endpoint, or something in front of it that holds a valid certificate for it (a proxy, load balancer or CDN), to issue the redirect. A passive network attacker cannot inject a redirect into an HTTPS session. What they gain is the ability to read the credentials once the endpoint has sent them over plaintext HTTP, or once it has sent them to a host it was never trusted with. ### Impact - **swift:** whoever receives the token can list, read, write and delete objects in the whole account until the token expires. The v1 API key and the v2/v3 password are long-lived credentials. - **seafile:** the API token gives full access to the account. The password can be used to log in. - **netstorage:** whoever receives the signature can replay the one signed request within the time window. ### Patches Fixed in rclone v1.76.0: - `fshttp`: rclone's HTTP transport refuses to follow a redirect from `https://` to `http://` and returns an error naming the new `--allow-https-downgrade` flag. Because the check is in the transport, it also covers clients that libraries build for themselves, such as the swift library's. Use `--allow-https-downgrade` to follow such redirects, for example when downloading from a mirror which redirects to plain HTTP. **This is a behaviour change:** the `http` backend and `rclone copyurl` used to follow these redirects silently. - `swift`: the transport rclone gives the library removes `X-Auth-Token`, `X-Auth-User` and `X-Auth-Key` once a redirect leaves the original host and port. It refuses an HTTPS to HTTP redirect, and a cross-host redirect which would resend the request body. - `netstorage`: the three `X-Akamai-ACS-*` headers are removed once a redirect leaves the original host and port, and HTTPS to HTTP redirects are refused. - `seafile`: HTTPS to HTTP redirects are refused for the API client and the configuration client. The swift, netstorage and seafile backends refuse a downgrade even when `--allow-https-downgrade` is set, because following it would send their credentials in cleartext. ### Workarounds Before upgrading, only use endpoints you trust not to redirect elsewhere. For swift that includes the storage URL returned by the auth server. Use `https://` endpoints, and never point these backends at a proxy that downgrades to HTTP. ### Credits Reported by zx (@manus-pi) as three separate reports, combined into this advisory.
